blocks.text: Watch a person walk down a corridor and you can often tell what is wrong before they speak: a foot that slaps down, a hip that sags, a knee pushed back by a hand. Each abnormal gait is a missing piece of the normal cycle, and the quickest way to find the missing piece is to know what each muscle does and when.

blocks.markdown: Walking is a repeated sequence of movements. The **gait cycle** is defined as the interval from one **heel strike** of a foot to the next heel strike of the **same** foot. Within it each leg alternates between supporting the body (the **stance phase**) and swinging forward (the **swing phase**). Because the cycle is repeated, we can describe it as a percentage of its total duration.

blocks.title: Stance and swing phases
blocks.text: The stance phase is the period when the foot is on the ground, from heel strike to toe off, and makes up about 60 percent of the gait cycle in normal walking. The swing phase is the period when the foot is off the ground and the limb moves forward, from toe off to the next heel strike, and makes up about 40 percent. For about 20 percent of the cycle in total both feet are on the ground (double support, two periods of about 10 percent each).

blocks.caption: Phases and subphases of the gait cycle.

Walking speed v is the stride length (distance covered in one gait cycle, in metres) divided by the stride time (duration of one cycle, in seconds). A step is half a stride: from one heel strike to the heel strike of the opposite foot.

blocks.title: Timing a gait cycle
blocks.prompt: A gait cycle lasts 1.2 s. Using stance as 60 percent of the cycle, calculate the duration of the swing phase.

steps.text: Swing is the remainder of the cycle after stance, so swing is 100 - 60 = 40 percent of the cycle.
Duration of swing = 0.40 x 1.2 s = 0.48 s.

blocks.answer: The swing phase lasts 0.48 s (and the stance phase 0.72 s).

blocks.markdown: **Muscles active in the cycle.** At the end of swing the **hamstrings** decelerate the forward-swinging leg, and the **quadriceps** and **gluteus maximus** prepare the limb to take weight. At **heel strike** the **tibialis anterior** (the dorsiflexor) contracts eccentrically to lower the forefoot to the ground gently; if it is weak the foot slaps down ('foot slap'). In early stance the **quadriceps** controls knee flexion and the **gluteus maximus** extends the hip. Throughout stance on one leg, **gluteus medius and minimus** keep the pelvis level. At **toe off** the **gastrocnemius and soleus** plantarflex the ankle to push the body forward, helped by the long toe flexors, and the hip flexors (**iliopsoas** and **rectus femoris**) begin to swing the leg forward. During swing the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus keep the toes clear of the floor.

blocks.title: Which muscle fails?
blocks.prompt: A patient's foot slaps on the ground just after heel strike and the toes drag during swing. Which muscle group is weak and what is its nerve?

steps.text: Foot slap at heel strike means the foot cannot be lowered in a controlled way, so the dorsiflexors are not controlling the movement.
Toe drag in swing means dorsiflexion is insufficient to clear the ground.
Dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL) are in the anterior compartment, supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

blocks.answer: The dorsiflexors of the anterior compartment, supplied by the deep fibular nerve (a foot drop gait).

rows: Foot cannot be lifted, so the knee is raised higher in swing
Unilateral weakness: Trendelenburg (abductor) lurch or limp; bilateral weakness: waddling gait
Pelvis drops on the unsupported side; trunk tilts (lurches) towards the weak side to bring the centre of gravity over the stance hip
Gluteus maximus gait (backward trunk lurch at heel strike)

Trunk is thrown backwards at heel strike so that the line of gravity passes behind the hip joint; this gives an extending moment from gravity itself, replacing the weak gluteus maximus, which cannot extend the hip
Knee pushed back by the hand
Patient presses on the thigh to keep the knee straight in stance
Cannot propel the body forward at toe off
blocks.caption: Characteristic abnormal gaits from weakness of a muscle group.

items: Gait cycle: heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot; stance about 60 percent, swing about 40 percent.
Heel strike: tibialis anterior controls the lowering of the foot.
Toe off: gastrocnemius and soleus plantarflex to push off.
Dorsiflexor weakness gives a high-stepping gait; gluteus medius weakness gives a Trendelenburg gait.

blocks.title: Percentages are typical values
blocks.text: The percentages of stance and swing are typical for normal, comfortable walking and change with walking speed. Faster walking shortens stance and double support; running removes double support entirely.

points: The gait cycle runs from heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot, with stance about 60 percent and swing about 40 percent.
Tibialis anterior controls foot lowering at heel strike, gastrocnemius and soleus push off at toe off, and gluteus medius keeps the pelvis level in stance.
Weakness of a muscle group produces a characteristic gait: foot drop gives a high-stepping gait, gluteus medius weakness a Trendelenburg gait, gluteus maximus weakness a backward lurch.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of the normal gait cycle is spent in the stance phase?

distractorRationale.b: About 40 percent is the swing phase.
distractorRationale.c: About 20 percent is the total double support time.
distractorRationale.d: This is much higher than normal walking.

questions.explanation: In normal walking the foot is on the ground for about 60 percent of the cycle (stance) and off the ground for about 40 percent (swing). The two limbs share the stance time, producing double support periods.

questions.stem: Which event marks the end of the stance phase and the start of swing?

distractorRationale.b: Heel strike marks the start of stance.
distractorRationale.c: Midstance is in the middle of stance.
distractorRationale.d: Foot flat occurs early in stance.

questions.explanation: The stance phase ends when the toes leave the ground at toe off. Swing then continues until the next heel strike of the same foot.

questions.stem: Which muscle contracts eccentrically at heel strike to lower the forefoot to the ground?

distractorRationale.c: Soleus is active in mid and late stance and at push-off.
distractorRationale.d: Iliopsoas flexes the hip to begin swing.

questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior, the main dorsiflexor, contracts eccentrically after heel strike to lower the foot gently. Weakness leads to foot slap.

questions.stem: Which muscles plantarflex the ankle to push the body forward at toe off?

options.text: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus

distractorRationale.d: These extend the knee and flex the hip.

questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius and soleus plantarflex the ankle at toe off, propelling the body forward. Weakness shortens the stride and reduces push-off.

questions.stem: A patient walks with the trunk thrown backwards at each heel strike on the right. Which muscle is most likely weak?

distractorRationale.b: Gluteus medius weakness causes pelvic drop on the opposite side.
distractorRationale.c: Tibialis anterior weakness causes foot slap and steppage.

questions.explanation: The gluteus maximus extends the hip at heel strike. When it is weak the patient throws the trunk backwards to keep the line of gravity behind the hip, producing a characteristic lurch.

questions.stem: A gait cycle lasts 1.0 s, and the stance phase is 60 percent of the cycle. How long, in seconds, is the swing phase?
questions.explanation: The swing phase is the part of the cycle that is not stance, so it is 100 minus 60, which is 40 percent of the cycle. Forty percent of 1.0 s is 0.4 s.

questions.stem: A person completes one gait cycle (one stride) covering a distance of 1.4 m in 1.0 s. Using walking speed as stride length divided by stride time, calculate the walking speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: Speed is stride length divided by stride time. Dividing 1.4 m by 1.0 s gives 1.4 m/s, a value that is typical of comfortable adult walking.

questions.stem: True or false: the gait cycle is measured from heel strike of one foot to heel strike of the opposite foot.

distractorRationale.a: Heel strike of one foot to heel strike of the opposite foot is a step, which is half a stride.

questions.explanation: The gait cycle runs from heel strike of one foot to the next heel strike of the same foot. The interval between heel strikes of opposite feet is a step, half of the cycle.

questions.stem: Divide the gait cycle into stance and swing phases and describe the subphases of each, giving the approximate percentage of each phase.
markingGuide: Gait cycle: heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot.
Stance about 60 percent: heel strike, foot flat, midstance, heel off, toe off.
Swing about 40 percent: acceleration, midswing, deceleration.
Double support is about 20 percent in total.
Describe what the limb does in each subphase.
questions.explanation: Stance and swing alternate in each limb, with both feet on the ground during double support. Naming subphases gives a framework for relating muscle activity to the events.

questions.stem: Explain how weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus produces a Trendelenburg gait, and contrast it with the gait produced by weakness of the dorsiflexors.
markingGuide: Gluteus medius and minimus of the stance leg normally keep the pelvis level.

When weak, the pelvis drops on the unsupported (opposite) side; the trunk tilts towards the weak side to compensate, producing a Trendelenburg lurch or limp (bilateral weakness gives a waddling gait).
Dorsiflexor weakness: foot slap at heel strike and toe drag in swing.
The patient raises the knee higher (steppage gait) to clear the toes.
Gluteal nerve is the superior gluteal nerve; dorsiflexors are supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
questions.explanation: The two gaits arise from failures at different points in the cycle: pelvic control in stance versus toe clearance in swing. Recognising which phase is affected points to the muscle group.
